title: Reading 400 Million Git Pushes: GitHub OSINT at Full Population
summary_en: A researcher reconstructed the entire 2025 GitHub public push stream into a queryable database, uncovering nearly 10,000 live credentials and widespread corporate data leaks from personal repositories.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability stems from a systemic 'blind spot' in GitHub's security architecture: secret scanning and push protection (tools that block secrets from being uploaded) only apply to repositories owned by an organization. When employees, contractors, or ex-employees push code to their personal public repositories, they often use their corporate email addresses or include sensitive files like .env or .pem, which are completely invisible to the employer's security team. This creates a massive third-party risk where corporate secrets are exposed in unmonitored personal spaces.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher used the GitHub Archive (a public record of every event on GitHub) to identify when a 'push' (sending code updates to a server) occurred.
2. Because the archive doesn't show what changed, they used the GitHub REST Compare API (a tool to see differences between two versions of code) to fetch the list of changed files for 405 million pushes.
3. They loaded this data into BigQuery (a powerful Google database for searching massive amounts of information) to make it searchable using SQL (a language for querying databases).
DISCOVERY
4. To find corporate identities, they searched for commit emails (the email address attached to a code change) that didn't belong to common providers like Gmail.
SELECT REGEXP_EXTRACT(author_email, r'@(.+)$') AS domain FROM `ghscan.commits_2025` WHERE author_email NOT LIKE '%gmail.com%';
Why: This extracts the domain (the part after the @) to identify employees from companies like NVIDIA or Microsoft committing to personal repos.
5. They filtered out 'bots' (automated programs) by looking for accounts with a massive number of pushes but very few repositories.
SELECT actor, COUNT(*) AS pushes FROM `ghscan.commits_2025` GROUP BY actor ORDER BY pushes DESC;
Why: High push counts on single repos usually indicate automated systems rather than human developers.
EXPLOITATION
6. The researcher searched for sensitive file paths (locations of files) that commonly contain secrets, such as .env (environment variables) or .pem (security keys).
SELECT repository, actor, f AS path FROM `ghscan.commits_2025`, UNNEST(files) AS f WHERE f LIKE '%.env' OR f LIKE '%.pem';
Why: Developers often accidentally include these files, which contain passwords or private keys, in their code uploads.
7. They identified 639,806 repositories containing .env files and tens of thousands with private keys (.pem) or cloud configuration files (.tfstate).
IMPACT
8. By checking the contents of these files (outside the database), they found 9,965 live credentials that still worked.
9. Among these were 22 AWS root keys (master keys for Amazon Cloud accounts) that had been public for over a year.
10. They discovered that corporate identities leak even when the code itself is harmless, allowing attackers to map out an organization's developers and their side projects.
lesson.example: Imagine a developer at 'target.example' is working on a personal side project at home. They use their work laptop and have their git configuration set to their work email (dev@target.example). They create a new project and accidentally include a file named '.env' which contains the production database password for target.example. They run 'git push' to their personal public GitHub account. An attacker queries a database like the one in the article for any commits where the email ends in '@target.example' and the file list includes '.env'. The attacker finds the repo, downloads the .env file, and uses the password to steal the company's entire customer database.
lesson.takeaway: Corporate security does not end at the organization's GitHub boundary; employee personal repositories are a primary leak vector. When hunting, don't just search for company names (which leads to false positives); search for corporate email domains in commit metadata. Look for specific high-value file extensions like .env, .tfstate, .pem, and .npmrc. A key variant is the 'CLAUDE.md' or 'AGENTS.md' files, which are used by AI coding assistants and can be manipulated for prompt injection. Avoid the mistake of assuming a deleted repository means the secret is gone; if it was indexed or archived, it is still findable.
lesson.fix: Organizations should implement a strict policy forbidding the use of corporate email addresses for personal GitHub accounts. Use tools like 'canary tokens' (fake secrets that alert you when used) to detect leaks early. Instead of relying on GitHub's built-in scanning, companies should use external OSINT tools to monitor the public push stream for their own domains and employee handles. Most importantly, secrets should never be stored in files; use a dedicated secret management service (like AWS Secrets Manager or HashiCorp Vault) where access is tied to identity, not a text string in a file. If a leak occurs, the only safe response is to revoke the credential entirely, as rotating it does not remove the historical exposure.

excerpt: > TL;DR > > > I’ve rebuilt the entire 2025 Personal Public GitHub push stream (405M pushes, 32.8M repos, 2.41B file paths) into a single queryable BigQuery table and measured what actually leaks at full population rather than from a sample. The dataset is available to anyone with a valid Google Cloud account: https://console.cloud.google.com/bigquery?ws=!1m4!1m3!3m2!1sghscan-corpus-12520!2sghscan > > > **Secrets that still work:**after removing the scanner noise we were left with 9,965 credentials that still authenticated (a floor), 57% of which were database logins. title: $19,500 for a Package Name That Didn’t Exist Yet: A Dependency Confusion Supply Chain Takeover
summary_en: A researcher earned $19,500 by identifying internal package names in a company's public GitHub repositories and registering those same names on a public registry to hijack their build pipeline.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability, known as Dependency Confusion, occurs when a company's build system (an automated process that compiles code) is configured to fetch packages (reusable code blocks) from both internal and public libraries. If a package name exists in both places, the system often defaults to the public version or the one with the higher version number. Hartwell Digital exposed their internal package names in public configuration files but failed to 'claim' or reserve those names on public registries like npm or PyPI.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher identified the target, Hartwell Digital, a fintech platform with public-facing code.
2. They used an LLM (Large Language Model—an AI tool that processes text) to scan the company's public GitHub repositories (online storage for code).
3. The researcher looked specifically for configuration files like package.json (a file listing a project's required code libraries).

DISCOVERY
4. Inside the package.json files, the researcher found names of 'internal' packages that were not available on the public internet.
5. They checked public registries (digital libraries where developers share code) to see if these specific names were available for anyone to register.
6. The researcher found a package name that 'didn't exist yet' on the public registry but was being called by the company's internal systems.

EXPLOITATION
7. The researcher registered the exact internal package name on the public registry.
8. They uploaded a benign 'placeholder' package to this name.
9. They assigned a very high version number to their public package (e.g., 99.9.9).

IMPACT
10. When Hartwell's build pipeline (the automated system that prepares the app for use) ran an install command, it checked the public registry.
11. Because the public registry had a 'newer' version (99.9.9) than the internal one, the system automatically downloaded the researcher's code.
12. This allowed the researcher's code to execute inside the company's secure build environment, proving they could have stolen data or sabotaged the software.
lesson.takeaway: This is a 'Supply Chain' attack because it targets the tools used to build the software rather than the software itself. To find these, always check public repositories for configuration files (package.json, requirements.txt, pom.xml) and cross-reference internal-looking names with public registries. A common variant is 'Typosquatting,' where an attacker registers a name very similar to a popular package (e.g., 'requesst' instead of 'requests'). Beginners often forget that even if a package is 'private,' the name itself must be protected globally.

excerpt: This bug never touched Hartwell’s actual application code, their servers, or anything resembling a traditional request-response exploit chain. The entire attack happened on a public package registry, days before anyone at the company would run the install command that quietly pulled my code into their build pipeline instead of their own. The target, which I’ll call **Hartwell Digital** here per their program’s anonymization terms, is a fintech platform with a large internal engineering org and, like most companies that size, a mix of open-source dependencies and internally-built packages used

title: The Verizon Report Just Proved Something Terrifying: Attackers Are Using AI to Exploit Bugs in…
summary_en: Researchers used AI to identify and exploit an unpatched image-processing library on OpenAI's forum server, gaining full remote control and internal code access.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability was caused by a 'missing backport' of a security patch in libheif, an image parsing library (a collection of pre-written code used to read image files). While a fix for a known security hole existed, the server's operating system (Debian) had not yet updated the library. This created a 'dependency version gap,' where the application relied on an old, insecure component, allowing attackers to use a known exploit (a tool used to take advantage of a bug) to gain control.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Researchers used AI to analyze Docker images (packages containing software and its environment) used by OpenAI.
`docker pull [openai-forum-image]`
Why: To inspect the exact versions of software libraries installed on the server to find outdated code.
2. The AI identified that the libheif library was missing a critical security patch (a software update that fixes a security hole).
`dpkg -l | grep libheif`
Why: To check the version of the image-parsing tool against a database of known vulnerabilities (a vulnerability is a weakness in code).
DISCOVERY
3. The researchers analyzed the specific code gap between the current version and the patched version.
`diff libheif_old.c libheif_patched.c`
Why: To understand exactly what code was changed in the fix, which reveals how to trigger the original bug (triggering means making the bug happen).
EXPLOITATION
4. AI was used to build a working exploit tailored to the server's specific architecture (the way the computer's hardware and software are organized).
`./exploit-builder --target libheif --arch x64`
Why: To create a custom 'payload' (malicious data) that forces the server to execute unauthorized commands.
5. The exploit was sent to the forum server, likely through an image upload endpoint (a specific web address on a server that receives data).
`POST /forum/upload HTTP/1.1` 
Why: To deliver the malicious image file to the vulnerable libheif library for processing.
IMPACT
6. The researchers gained Remote Code Execution (RCE), allowing them to run any command on the server.
`whoami` 
Why: To prove they have control over the system (RCE is a bug that lets you run your own code on a remote computer).
7. From the forum server, they moved laterally (moving from one compromised system to another) to access internal code repositories.
`git clone https://internal-repo.openai.com/` 
Why: To demonstrate that a single unpatched library can lead to the exposure of sensitive company secrets.
lesson.example: A fictional website target.example allows users to upload profile pictures. The site uses an old version of 'ImageMagick' (a library for editing images). An attacker discovers this version has a bug called 'ImageTragick.' The attacker creates a text file disguised as an image containing the payload: `fill 'url(https://example.com/"|touch /tmp/hacked")'`. When the server tries to 'resize' this fake image, it accidentally runs the `touch` command, creating a file on the server. This works because the server didn't check if the image content was safe before letting the library process it.
lesson.takeaway: Always check the versions of third-party libraries (dependencies) used by a target, especially those that process complex files like images, PDFs, or videos. Use tools like 'nuclei' or 'retire.js' to identify outdated components. A common signal is a server running an older operating system version which may have delayed security updates. A variant of this is 'Dependency Confusion,' where attackers trick a system into downloading a malicious library instead of a real one. A common beginner mistake is assuming that if a website looks modern, its underlying server software is also up-to-date.
lesson.fix:
The correct fix is to implement an automated dependency scanning process using tools like Snyk, GitHub Dependabot, or OWASP Dependency-Check. These tools automatically flag outdated libraries and suggest updates. In this specific case, the fix involved updating the operating system packages to ensure the patched version of libheif was installed.

```bash
# Update package lists and upgrade the specific vulnerable library
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install --only-upgrade libheif1
```

title: ArtiPACKED: Hacking Giants Through a Race Condition in GitHub Actions Artifacts
program: GitHub, Google (Firebase), Microsoft, AWS, Red Hat, Canonical (Ubuntu Adsys), OWASP
summary_en: Unit 42's ArtiPACKED research abused a race condition in GitHub Actions workflow artifacts to leak GitHub and cloud tokens from public repos of Red Hat, Google, AWS, Microsoft, Canonical and OWASP, enabling repo compromise and potential cloud access.
summary_ar: بحث ArtiPACKED من Unit 42 استغل Race Condition في GitHub Actions workflow artifacts لتسريب توكنات GitHub وسحابة من ريبوهات عامة لـ Red Hat وGoogle وAWS وMicrosoft وCanonical وOWASP، ما كان ممكن يسمح باختراق الريبوهات والوصول للبيئات السحابية.

lesson.cause_ar: الـ root cause إن فرق التطوير بتعامل مع workflow artifacts على GitHub Actions كأنها مخرجات build عادية ومؤقتة من غير أي credential hygiene، بينما هي في الحقيقة بتتسرب منها توكنات — سواء توكنات خدمات سحابية تبع طرف تالت أو GitHub tokens — وأي حد عنده read access على الريبو يقدر يستهلكها. الافتراض الغلط إن الـ artifacts مش حساسة ومش متاحة لغير المطوّرين، لكن في الريبوهات العامة أي حد في العالم يقدر يفتحها. ووجود Race Condition في طريقة تعامل GitHub Actions مع الـ artifacts خلّى نافذة الاستغلال أوسع، وده بيتماشى مع OWASP CICD-SEC-06 (Insufficient Credential Hygiene) اللي المقال بيستشهد بيه كأحد أهم مخاطر الـ CI/CD.
lesson.walkthrough_ar: الباحث Yaron Avital كان متابع حدسه إن في feature مهملة اسمها workflow artifacts على GitHub — المنصة اللي بتستضيف أغلب المشاريع مفتوحة المصدر — وقرر يفحصها. بدأ يستكشف الـ artifacts اللي بتتولّد من workflows الـ CI/CD في ريبوهات عامة لشركات كبيرة، وكان مقتنع إنه هيّلاقي sensitive data أو credentials. النتيجة كانت أكبر من اللي كان متخيله: لقى إن الـ artifacts بتسرّب توكنات، سواء توكنات خدمات سحابية تبع طرف تالت أو GitHub tokens، وكلها متاحة لأي حد عنده read access على الريبو. أكثر تسريب شائع كان GitHub tokens، وده بيخوّل المهاجم يتصرف باسم الريبو اللي شغّل الـ workflow نفسه. من هنا يقدر يدفع malicious code يتدفق للإنتاج عبر الـ CI/CD pipeline، أو يقرا secrets مخزنة في الريبو والـ organization. البحث كشف مشاريع مفتوحة المصدر معروفة جدًا مملوكة لـ Red Hat وGoogle (Firebase) وAWS وMicrosoft وCanonical (Ubuntu Adsys) وOWASP. كل الحالات اتبلّغت للمسؤولين عن المشاريع، وكل الفرق تعاونت بسرعة عشان يخففوا الأثر. التقنية الأساسية اللي اتعملت عليها التسمية ArtiPACKED هي Race Condition في طريقة تعامل GitHub Actions مع الـ artifacts، وده اللي وسّع تأثير التسريب من مجرد توكنات لاختراق محتمل للبيئات السحابية.
lesson.takeaway_ar: أي وقت تشتغل على هدف فيه CI/CD على GitHub، نزّل workflow artifacts من الـ runs وافحصها بـ grep على أنماط التوكنات المعروفة (ghp_, AKIA, AIza وغيرها). دور على الـ workflows اللي بتستخدم secrets وبعدين بتعمل upload-artifact، وافحص مدة الاحتفاظ بالـ artifacts وإعدادات الوصول ليها. النمط ده بيتكرر في أي نظام بيخزّن مخرجات build وبيستهلكها بعدين عمليات بصلاحيات أعلى — والـ race condition في التعامل مع الملفات المؤقتة دي علامة إن في حاجة ممكن تستغلها. كمان ركّز على الريبوهات العامة لأن الـ read access فيها متاح لأي حد، فالتسريب بيبقى متاح للجميع مش بس للموظفين.
lesson.fix_ar: الحل الصح مش بس إنهم مسحوا الـ artifacts — لازم من الأساس ممنوع تخزين أي secret جوه artifact؛ استخدم secret manager أو OIDC tokens قصيرة العمر بدل التوكنات طويلة العمر في الـ workflows. فعّل retention قصير للـ artifacts وقيّد الوصول ليها، وضيف فحص تلقائي للـ secrets على أي ملف بيتعمل له upload-artifact قبل ما يخرج من الـ pipeline. وده بالظبط اللي بيقوله OWASP CICD-SEC-06 عن credential hygiene: افصل صلاحيات الـ build عن صلاحيات الإنتاج، وخلّي أي توكن يشتغل بأقل privilege ممكن.
